transcript.text: hotpoint SA2 oven not heatin on fan, grill ok. wat does SA2 mean??

## What "SA2" means

On Hotpoint built-in ovens, the model code breaks down roughly like this:

• S = Single oven (a double oven would start with D, e.g. DD2…)
• A = a range/design series letter
• 2 = Class 2, Hotpoint's entry-level built-in range (Class 3, 4, 6 and so on are higher up)

So an SA2 540 H IX, for example, is a Class 2 single built-in oven. The rest of the code covers the specific features and finish (IX = stainless steel).

## Fan oven not heating, grill fine

The grill works, so the oven is getting power. The fault is in the fan-oven circuit. The usual culprits, from most to least likely:

1. Fan oven element blown (most common). This is the round element hidden behind the back panel of the oven cavity. Symptom: the fan spins but there's no heat.
2. Fan motor failed. Symptom: no fan noise or movement at all. Many ovens won't heat properly in fan mode if the fan isn't running.
3. Thermal cut-out tripped or failed. This often cuts several functions at once.
4. Selector switch or thermostat faulty. This is less common.

### Quick checks
• Turn it to fan mode and look and listen. Is the fan turning?
• Fan spins but no heat → almost certainly the element.
• No fan → fan motor (or its wiring).
• Try conventional mode (top and bottom heat, no fan) if your oven has it. If that heats, the problem is isolated to the fan element or fan.

### Fixing it
• Switch off at the wall isolator first. Don't rely on the oven controls being off.
• The fan element is usually a cheap part, often about £15–30. Search your full model number from the rating plate on the door edge or frame.
• To check the element, unscrew the back panel inside the oven. You'll typically need to slide the oven out of its housing to reach the wiring connections at the back.
• With a multimeter, a good element usually reads about 20–30 ohms. An open circuit (no reading) means it's dead.

If you're not comfortable working on mains wiring, a local appliance engineer can usually do an element swap quickly and fairly cheaply.

Tell me whether the fan spins in fan mode and I can help narrow it down further.
fan isnt spinning, just a low hum from the back. it was noisy for a few weeks before (squealing/grinding at startup). conventional heat works but only slowly

## Diagnosis: seized fan motor

Weeks of squealing and grinding at startup, then a hum with no spin, is the classic sign of worn-out fan motor bearings. The bearings have now seized. The motor is still getting power (the hum) but can't turn.

The fan element itself is probably fine. You just won't get proper fan-oven heat without air moving across it.

### Quick confirmation
1. Switch off at the wall isolator and let the oven cool.
2. Reach in and gently turn the fan blade at the back by hand (you may need to remove the back panel to reach it).
• Stiff, gritty, or won't move → seized motor, confirmed.
• Spins freely → less likely, but could be a failed motor capacitor/winding or a wiring issue.

Don't keep running fan mode in the meantime. A stalled motor drawing current can overheat, and it can trip the thermal cut-out and take other functions down with it.

### About conventional being slow
Top and bottom heat is naturally slower to preheat than fan, so some slowness is normal. But if it's much slower than it used to be, check that both elements are working. After 10 minutes on conventional, the top of the cavity and the oven floor area should both be clearly hot. If one stays cool, that element may have failed too.

### Fixing it
Part: a replacement fan motor, usually around £20–45. Match it using the full model number and the code on the rating plate (on the door edge or frame). Some motors come with a new blade; if yours doesn't, reuse the old one.

Rough steps:
1. Isolate the power at the wall.
2. Remove the back panel inside the oven cavity.
3. Remove the fan blade nut. On many Hotpoint/Indesit ovens this is a left-hand (reverse) thread, so turn it clockwise to undo. Hold the blade firmly and don't force it the wrong way.
4. Slide the oven out of its housing and remove the rear cover.
5. Photograph the wiring, then disconnect the motor wires.
6. Unscrew the motor (usually 3 screws or nuts) and fit the new one in reverse order.
7. Refit the blade and check it spins freely before reassembling.

It's a common, very doable DIY job if you're comfortable with basic mains appliance work. If not, an engineer will typically do it quickly, and with the part cost being low it's usually well worth repairing rather than replacing the oven.
isolated it at the cooker switch n tried the blade by hand, its very stiff n gritty. also got a slight hot smell from the back once but not now

## Confirmed: seized fan motor

Stiff and gritty by hand, plus the earlier grinding and humming, means the motor bearings have failed. A new fan motor is the fix. Bearings can't really be repaired on these, and lubricating them would only buy a short time.

## About the hot smell

That was almost certainly the stalled motor overheating. A motor that's powered but can't turn draws extra current and heats its windings. Since it's stopped, it's not an emergency, but:

• Don't use fan mode at all until the motor is replaced.
• Conventional mode should be fine to use meanwhile, as the fan normally isn't powered in that mode. Keep an eye (and nose) on it.
• If the smell comes back, or you smell burning plastic or see smoke, switch off at the isolator and leave it off until it's repaired.

When you have the back off, look at the motor's wiring connectors. If any are browned, melted, or the insulation is brittle, replace those connectors or that bit of wiring too. Heat damage there can cause problems later.

## Getting the right part

1. Find the rating plate (door edge or frame) and note the full model number and the service/product code (often a long number).
2. Search "[model number] fan motor". Genuine or good-quality pattern parts both work.
3. Check whether it comes with a blade. If not, you'll reuse yours.

## Finishing the fitting (from where I left off)

7. Refit the blade and nut (remember: likely reverse thread, so tighten anticlockwise). Spin it by hand to check it turns freely and doesn't catch.
8. Refit the rear cover, slide the oven back in, and refit the back panel inside the cavity.
9. Power up, run fan mode, and check that the fan spins quietly and the oven heats normally.

A bit of smell on the first run can be normal from new parts or burning off residue. It should fade quickly.

## If something else fails afterwards

If you lose several functions at once after all this, the thermal cut-out may have tripped or failed because of the overheating. It's a cheap part, usually near the top-rear of the oven.

If you'd rather not do the wiring yourself, an appliance engineer can typically swap a fan motor in under an hour.
